paper_title: AgSpec: Pushing the Limits of Retrieval-Based Speculative Decoding in Coding Agent Pipelines

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Retrieval-based speculative decoding (SD) drafts tokens by copying continuations from existing text, which suits coding agents that repeatedly reproduce code, logs, and earlier attempts. Yet existing methods fall short in agent pipelines: much of the reusable text is missing from their corpora or stored in a form that differs from what the agent emits, and their draft lengths ignore that accept length varies across agents and drifts over turns. We present AgSpec, a framework that supplies the corpus and draft-length policies that existing retrieval engines lack in coding-agent pipelines. AgSpec retrieves from session, workspace, and global corpora, retaining the ongoing session trajectory and indexing opened files in the agent's emission format. It bounds each agent's draft length with an offline-profiled cap and adapts the length online from verification feedback. On two repository-level multi-agent coding benchmarks, AgSpec outperforms five retrieval-based drafters and EAGLE-3 in most evaluated settings, raising generation throughput over autoregressive decoding up to 4.37$\times$ at batch size 1 and 4.76$\times$ at batch size 16. AgSpec also remains effective on benchmarks without a repository or a multi-agent pipeline, showing that its gains generalize to coding agents broadly.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Coding agents have become representative LLM application (Liu et al., 2026a). Unlike chatbot, coding agent handles single user request as multi-turn session that alternates between model calls and tool execution (Yang et al., 2024). Within session, the work is often divided among specialized agents, such as coder that edits files and an executor that runs tests and scripts to check the result (Hong et al., 2024). As user requests have shifted from synthesizing single function (Chen et al., 2021) to resolving repository-level issues (Jimenez et al., 2024), agents rarely succeed in one pass and instead refine their attempts over multiple turns (Madaan et al., 2023). Each additional turn can improve the output, but it also lengthens the time user waits for the result (Tiwari et al., 2026). Speculative decoding (SD) attacks this cost directly, reducing decoding latency without changing the output (Chen et al., 2023). In SD, drafter proposes several tokens, and the target model verifies them in parallel and commits the accepted tokens. Each accepted token saves sequential targetmodel step. This saving comes at the cost of generating draft tokens and verifying tokens that are later rejected. Rejected tokens are nearly free at small batch sizes but become expensive at large batch sizes, where verification demands much more compute (Liu et al., 2024; Sadhukhan et al., 2025). SD thus pays off only when the drafter is both cheap and accurate. Existing designs range from small draft models (Leviathan et al., 2023) and trained draft heads (Li et al., 2025) to retrievalbased SD, which retrieves draft tokens from text corpus. Retrieval-based SD is particularly effective for code generation (Liu et al., 2026b). It copies continuations from text the system already has, such as the current prompt, earlier responses, or prebuilt datastore, without running separate draft model. Code suits this copying, since identifiers, code fragments, and repository conventions recur, and coding-agent sessions offer still more of it, as repeated subtasks and refinement loops produce long, predictable sequences. However, previous

sections.content: Figure 1: (a) Accept length when restoring availability, then matchability. (b) Achievable accept length for Gemma3-27B, taking the best available continuation at each step. Markers are medians and bars the interquartile range. (c) Decoding throughput of SAM-Decoding and AGSPEC-SAM relative to no speculation for Gemma3-27B. All data is from SWE-bench Verified. works do not elicit the full performance of retrieval-based SD at coding agents. They overlook what makes coding agent different, and leave much of that reuse out of reach. draft helps only if two conditions hold: the text the agent reuses must be available in the corpus, and it must be matchable against what the agent generates. Existing corpora fall short on both. First, they limit availability: they hold either prebuilt datastore or the text of the current call, whereas coding agents reuse text from the ongoing session and the repository. file drops out of reach once the prompt truncates it, and retry cannot draw on the previous attempt once its call ends; covering these requires corpora that span the session and the repository. Second, they limit matchability: they store text as the agent read it, yet coder emits patch whose copied lines each carry diff prefix absent from the file. Fig. 1(a) shows that expanding retrieval scope raises accept length on every model, with the largest gain from session history and smaller additional headroom from repository history and emission-form indexing. Even when reusable match exists, choosing the draft length remains critical, as it directly determines how many drafted tokens are rejected. Existing methods fix the draft length policy before session runs, deriving it from static cap (Saxena, 2023; Hu et al., 2025; He et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025) or from properties of the match such as its length (Oliaro et al., 2025) or occurrence count (He et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Oliaro et al., 2025). However, in coding agents, the achievable accept length follows the agent pipeline. Fig. 1(b) shows that each agent occupies distinct accept-length range that shifts differently across and within turns. Each agent and context thus has characteristic accept length, which can guide the draft length better than fixed or match-derived policy. These limitations stem not from how existing methods match text but from the policies around the matching. retrieval-based SD method pairs retrieval engine that finds continuation for the current context (e.g., suffix tree in SuffixDecoding (Oliaro et al., 2025)) with policies that decide what the corpus holds and how many tokens to draft. Existing policies are built around the individual request, the unit an inference engine serves: they index the current call, prebuilt datastore, or outputs pooled across requests (Saxena, 2023; He et al., 2024; Oliaro et al., 2025), and size drafts by static cap or the match itself. In coding agent, however, reuse and acceptance depend on structure above the request, namely the session, the repository, and the role of each agent. We present AGSPEC, retrieval-based SD framework that builds its policies on this structure while leaving the engine unchanged, so it applies to existing engines as is. AGSPEC realizes each policy with simple yet effective design. (1) Coding-agent-aware retrieval. For the corpus, AGSPEC organizes text by origin into session, workspace, and global reference corpora. The workspace corpus indexes the artifacts session opens, in full and in the forms the agent emits. (2) Agentaware draft-length control. For the draft length, AGSPEC profiles agent-specific accept lengths offline to set per-agent draft caps, and learns draft-length scale that adapts the length per turn and per request from verification feedback. We compare AGSPEC against AR decoding, five retrieval-based SD methods (Saxena, 2023; He et al., 2024; Oliaro et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025), and EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025) on two repository-level benchmarks, SWE-bench and TeamBench (Jimenez et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026). AGSPEC consistently outperforms most baselines. Especially, with SAM-Decoding as its retrieval engine, AGSPEC raises the speedup of Gemma3-27B on SWE-bench over AR decoding from 2.72 to 3.61 at batch size 16  (Fig. 4)  . sections.title: 2.1 CODING AGENTS
sections.content: Coding agents resolve software engineering tasks by handling each user request as session (Jimenez et al., 2024). session may span several agents, each of which alternates between model calls and tool executions. Throughout the session, agents operate on persistent workspace: the repository checkout together with its execution environment. The workspace holds the artifacts agents work on, such as repository files, patches, and tool outputs. Unlike conversation history, artifacts are workspace state; in particular, most repository files predate the session and outlive it. However, what the workspace holds differs from what model call sees: each prompt exposes only the artifacts the scaffold selects, often truncated to fit the context length (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). Even when an agent reuses workspace text, its output rarely reproduces it verbatim. An agent reads an artifact as it stands but writes it back in the scaffolds emission format. Under unified-diff editing (Free Software Foundation, 2026), call emits header naming the file, followed by kept lines prefixed with space and removed lines prefixed with minus, so every line copied from the artifact begins with character the artifact does not contain  (Fig. 2)  . The code is identical, but the token sequence differs, so text indexed as the agent read it may not match what the agent generates. Other scaffolds emit whole files, search-and-replace blocks, or line-addressed edit commands (Xia et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024), and the choice measurably affects editing quality (Gauthier, 2023). Because the format is property of the scaffold, it is known before the session runs. The extent to which calls output repeats earlier text also depends on what the call does and when it is made. Within session, each model call is issued by an agent, serves role, and belongs to turn. Roles are the functions session performs, and each generates different kind of text: localizer names paths, coder rewrites files the session has already read, and an executor reproduces test logs. role describes what call does rather than which agent issues it: multi-agent systems assign each role to specialized agent (Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Phan et al., 2024), whereas others fix roles as pipeline stages (Xia et al., 2025) or interleave them within one agents loop (Yang et al., 2024). turn comprises solution attempt and its execution feedback, possibly spanning several roles; failed attempts trigger further turns until the task completes or retry limit is reached (Yang et al., 2024). Across turns, agents return to the same files and repeat much of the previous attempt. Roles thus determine what kind of text call generates, and turns determine how much of it repeats. Figure 2: The same code in two forms: as the workspace holds it, and as unified-diff patch emits it. Red marks the prefix each copied line gains. 2.2 RETRIEVAL-BASED SPECULATIVE DECODING Retrieval-based SD obtains drafts from existing text rather than draft model: it matches suffix of the decoding context, such as the prompt and generated prefix, against corpus and copies the continuation that follows. Its effectiveness hinges on two design choices. The corpus scope, which text is indexed and how long it is retained, determines whether useful match exists. The draft length, how many matched tokens are proposed, determines how many of them are rejected. Existing methods differ in both what their corpora index and how long they retain it. Request-local corpora last for single call. PLD searches the current prompt and generated prefix (Saxena, 2023), and SAM-Decoding and SuffixDecoding build per-request suffix automaton or tree over the prompt and output (Hu et al., 2025; Oliaro et al., 2025). Prebuilt corpora are assembled before serving and stay fixed. REST retrieves from text or code datastore (He et al., 2024), SAM-Decoding pairs its request-local automaton with static datastore (Hu et al., 2025), and FastCoder adds repository-local

sections.content: Figure 3: Overview of AGSPEC. Retrieval consults the session, workspace, and global corpora. Verification extends the output, updates the session corpus, and provides feedback to the length controller. The workspace corpus grows as artifacts are opened and is discarded when the session ends. files to common code (Zhao et al., 2025). few corpora persist across requests: SuffixDecoding keeps global tree of past responses (Oliaro et al., 2025; Snowflake Inc., 2026), and FastCoder caches verified and generated sequences (Zhao et al., 2025). Draft lengths are either fixed or scaled by the match. PLD and SAM-Decoding cap each continuation at fixed length, and REST uses fixed tree length (Saxena, 2023; Hu et al., 2025; He et al., 2024). SuffixDecoding scales its length with match length by configured factor (Oliaro et al., 2025), so its draft length varies with the input, but the factor itself is set before serving. These methods accelerate both code generation and agent workloads (He et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Oliaro et al., 2025), yet they remain limited in the agentic setting. First, agents reuse text from both the ongoing session and the repository workspace, and emit it in the scaffolds emission format. corpus should therefore span both sources and index text in that format, yet existing methods each cover only some of these sources. Second, their draft lengths ignore the contexts that shape acceptance: they are fixed (Saxena, 2023; He et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025) or scaled by preset factor (Oliaro et al., 2025), never corrected by verification outcomes, and blind to roles and turns. AGSPEC addresses these limitations with sourceand emission-aware corpus (3.1) and an adaptive draft length (3.2).

sections.title: 3 AGSPEC DESIGN
sections.content: AGSPEC is retrieval-based SD framework for coding agents that builds on an existing retrieval engine. retrieval engine finds the longest suffix match of the decoding context in corpus and returns its continuation, using an index such as the suffix automaton in SAM-Decoding (Hu et al., 2025) or the suffix tree in SuffixDecoding (Oliaro et al., 2025). AGSPEC operates on top of the engine without modifying it, so it applies to any engine that can search multiple corpora and accept per-step draft length. AGSPEC combines corpora organized by token source (3.1) with verificationdriven draft-length control (3.2). Fig. 3 depicts the overview of AGSPEC. 3.1 CODING-AGENT-AWARE RETRIEVAL AGSPEC addresses the corpus gap by indexing the reusable text in separate corpora keyed by source. Three mechanisms build on this separation: each corpus captures one source of reusable text, workspace artifacts are indexed in the forms the agent emits, and preference order ranks matches across corpora by how closely their source relates to the active session. Three corpora by source. AGSPEC maintains one corpus per source of reusable text. The session corpus Ss holds the text of session s, including prompts, tool outputs, and generated tokens, and is shared across its calls and agents, so text from earlier calls and turns remains retrievable. The workspace corpus Wr holds the repository artifacts opened during the current session and grows as additional artifacts are accessed. The global corpus holds large body of static reference text that is not specific to the current session; it is assembled before serving and stays fixed. These corpora are kept separate because their provenance and lifetime differ: the session and workspace corpora,

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: which we call live, are constructed within the current session and discarded when it ends, whereas the global corpus remains fixed across sessions. Indexing artifacts in emission form. Covering the workspace is not enough if its text no longer matches what the agent generates. The first time call opens an artifact, AGSPEC adds it to Wr in two forms. It adds the file as is, so the file remains retrievable even after truncation drops it from the prompt. It also adds the file as the agent would write it: because unified-diff patch prefixes kept lines with space and removed lines with minus  (Fig. 2)  , AGSPEC adds one copy with every line prefixed by space and another with every line prefixed by minus. Any line the coder copies into its patch thus matches one of these copies. scaffold that writes whole files through tool call instead needs one extra copy: the file as that call encodes it, with its newlines and quotes escaped. Later calls in the session reuse these entries instead of reindexing the file. Preferring matches by source. The retrieval engine queries each corpus with the same suffix of the decoding context and reports its longest match length mS , mW , and mG. Following prior retrievalbased SD (Oliaro et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025), AGSPEC treats longer match as better draft source, since more of the recent context agrees with the corpus text. Between the two live corpora, the longer match wins, with ties going to the session, whose text reflects the ongoing session. The global corpus must beat the live match by margin δ, because its text is plentiful and unrelated to the repository, so longer match there is likely coincidental. Formally, AGSPEC drafts from only when mG > max(mS , mW ) + δ; otherwise, it drafts from Ss if mS mW , and from Wr if not. includes δ sweep study. Continuation selection. Within the chosen corpus, match may occur at multiple positions with different continuations, so AGSPEC must select one occurrence. For both the global corpus and the session corpus Ss, AGSPEC groups occurrences by their next three tokens and selects the most frequent group, breaking ties by the most recent occurrence. For the workspace corpus Wr, it selects the first occurrence. includes the detailed analysis. Together, these mechanisms let AGSPEC draft from text that existing corpora miss: the sessions own outputs and whole workspace files in the agents emission format, while preferring the source most relevant to the ongoing session. 3.2 AGENT-AWARE DRAFT-LENGTH CONTROL draft token saves decoding step if accepted but wastes verification if rejected, waste that grows with batch size as verification becomes compute-bound. The draft length should therefore track how likely each token is to be accepted, which existing methods misjudge in two ways. static cap ignores that accept length differs across agents and drifts across and within turns (Fig. 1(b)). Match-derived rules (Oliaro et al., 2025) size the length by the match alone, regardless of which agent emits it or when. Both over-draft where acceptance is short. AGSPEC instead estimates the draft length from two sources: an offline-profiled cap for stable differences across agents, and an online scale that adjusts it to runtime drift from verification feedback. This cuts rejected tokens at small cost in accepted ones, raising throughput most at large batch sizes. Overview. The drafter copies up to Ki tokens that follow the match, so the actual draft length is Di = min{Ki, ℓi}, where ℓi is the number of tokens available after the match. Verification returns the accept length Ai, excluding tokens generated directly by the target model. As some retrieval engines, such as SuffixDecoding (Oliaro et al., 2025), have their own draft length control policy, AGSPEC uses the smaller value for the draft length between our policy and theirs. max Offline profiling of Kmax. sections.title: 4 EVALUATION
sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Models. We evaluate Devstral-24B (Mistral AI & All Hands AI, 2025), Gemma3-27B (Gemma Team, 2025), and Qwen3.6-27B (Qwen Team, 2026). Benchmarks. Our main evaluation uses two repository-level benchmarks, SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024) and TeamBench (Kim et al., 2026). On SWE-bench Verified, five agents localizer, coder, executor, reviewer, and summarizerrun in containers for up to five turns, with the coder editing repository files through unified diffs. TeamBench provides each task with repository workspace and spans eighteen task families, including code review, incident response, and infrastructure changes. planner, executor, and verifier proceed through planning, execution, and verification, with up to 20 turns per phase and two remediation loops, capped at 30 LLM calls per session. We additionally evaluate AGSPEC on LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025) and TerminalBench (Merrill et al., 2026) to separately test generality: LiveCodeBench has no repository, while Terminal-Bench uses single agent for all roles (4.3). We measure generation throughput excluding prefill and accept length (AL) for all benchmarks. Baselines. We compare autoregressive (AR) decoding, PLD (Saxena, 2023), REST (He et al., 2024), FastCoder (Zhao et al., 2025), SuffixDecoding (Oliaro et al., 2025), SAM-Decoding (Hu et al., 2025), and EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025). We follow the draft-length settings in the original papers, with configuration and implementation details reported in A. FastCoder extends REST with project datastore, cache of verified drafts and model output, and rule that skips retrieval where it rarely succeeds; we attach its project datastore on both SWE-bench Verified and TeamBench. AGSPEC Implementation. We implement AGSPEC in vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) over two retrieval engines: the suffix automaton of SAM-Decoding (AGSPEC-SAM) (Hu et al., 2025) and the suffix tree of SuffixDecoding (AGSPEC-Suffix) (Oliaro et al., 2025). Both engines use the same corpus configuration, draft-length controller, per-agent caps, and workspace scope, differing only in the underlying retrieval structure. For AGSPEC-SAM, we use frequency-majority continuation selection at both batch sizes. The maximum draft length is 64 at batch size 1 and 24 at batch size 16 for both implementations. Detailed configuration is at A.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 4: Main comparison across two repository benchmarks and three models. Rows show generation throughput and AL at batch sizes 1 and 16; higher is better. The number above each bar is its ratio to the no-speculation bar in that panel. no spec. denotes AR generation. Corpus construction. For each benchmark, we construct the global corpus from agent turn logs collected on disjoint set of coding tasks before evaluation. We use 70 tasks from SWE-bench Verified and 213 from TeamBench, indexing generated text and tool calls rendered in each models native format. Evaluation tasks are held out from corpus construction. 4.2 MAIN EVALUATION Fig. 4 compares AGSPEC with autoregressive decoding and six prior speculative methods on SWEbench Verified and TeamBench, using three models at batch sizes 1 and 16. Within each panel, all methods share the same workload and serving configuration. AGSPEC achieves the highest or the second highest throughput in all evaluated settings, reaching 2.274.37 the throughput of autoregressive decoding at batch size 1 and 1.084.76 at batch size 16. On average, its throughput is 18.0% higher than that of the fastest prior method. The gains are largest with Devstral at batch size 1 on SWE-bench Verified, achieving 1.36 higher than the fastest prior work. AGSPEC also achieves the highest AL in most evaluated settings. This demonstrates the effectiveness of AGSPEC for coding agents. Because AGSPEC runs on top of the retrieval engine, we also evaluate each engine with and without it. Both engines benefit in most settings. With SuffixDecoding, throughput rises by 16.5% on average and AL by 18.5%; with SAM-Decoding, throughput rises by 64.6% and AL nearly doubles. The gap reflects what each engine already provides. SuffixDecoding keeps tree of past responses and scales its draft with the match length, whereas SAM-Decoding does neither. Thus, although SAM-Decoding trails SuffixDecoding in all twelve settings, AGSPEC-SAM outperforms it in nine. These results show that existing retrieval engines, on their own, leave much of the speedup available in coding-agent pipelines untapped and AGSPEC, as framework, accelerates existing retrieval engines in coding-agent pipelines without modification. 4.3 NON-REPOSITORY AND IMPLICIT-AGENT TESTS AGSPEC primarily targets repository-level coding tasks performed by multi-agent systems. In practice, however, coding workloads also include simpler scenarios, such as standalone code generation or single-agent pipelines like ReAct (Yao et al., 2023). To evaluate whether AGSPEC generalizes to these settings, Fig. 5 shows its performance without repository workspace or explicit agent roles.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 5: Non-repository and single-agent evaluation at batch size 1 across three models. LiveCodeBench evaluates AGSPEC without repository context, using the global reference and session corpora with an empty workspace corpus. Terminal-Bench evaluates AGSPEC when agent functions are not represented by separate explicit roles. On LiveCodeBench, coder and feedback agent work on each problem for up to five turns without repository. Across the three models, the faster AGSPEC variant reaches 4.877.94 the generation throughput of autoregressive decoding and exceeds the fastest prior speculative method by 35145%. Its accept length also exceeds that of the prior method with the highest accept length. Although the workspace corpus is unavailable, AGSPEC can still retrieve from the global corpus and text accumulated within the session, while its draft-length controller continues to adapt from verification feedback, yielding these gains. On Terminal-Bench, single Terminus agent inspects files, takes actions, and interprets feedback without separate role assignments. The faster AGSPEC variant improves throughput over the fastest prior speculative method by 9.327.2%, while its accept length is 16.734.3% higher than that of its corresponding retrieval-engine baseline. For draft-length control, AGSPEC uses shared cap and single α table instead of role-specific caps, updating the scale from verification feedback. Thus, AGSPEC can improve decoding even when the workflow has only one explicit agent. Together, these results show that AGSPEC applies to broader range of coding agents. 4.4 ANALYSIS 4.4.1 IMPACT OF CODING-AGENT-AWARE RETRIEVAL We measure the contribution of coding-agent-aware retrieval through trace-driven simulation. In particular, we examine two design choices: using three corpora from different sources and indexing artifacts based on emission format. We replay the drafter over traces of AGSPEC-SAM sessions on SWE-bench Verified under each corpus configuration and compare the expected AL  (Fig. 6)  . Figure 6: Corpus ablation on SWE-bench Verified at batch size 1. (a) AL as corpora are added; the number above each bar is its ratio to alone, and Ccall is per-call corpus of the current prompt and output. (b) Coder AL gain per turn from indexing workspace artifacts in emission form, relative to raw file text only. Fig. 6(a) adds corpora to the global corpus one at time. Retaining text across calls gives the largest gain: replacing per-call corpus with the session corpus raises AL by 1.62.1, as agents repeatedly reproduce code and outputs from earlier calls. The workspace corpus adds 2647% on its own and

sections.content: still 2.27.0% on top of the session corpus, bringing AGSPEC to 2.94.8 the AL of the global corpus alone. This shows that each source contributes significantly to the system. Fig. 6(b) shows that emission-form indexing helps most in the first turn, raising the coders AL by 1339% before its own patches enter the session corpus. From the second turn on, those patches already supply the emitted form, so the gain falls to 3% or less by the fifth turn. Together, these results show that the session corpus supplies most of the reuse, while the workspace corpus and its emission forms cover what the session has not yet accumulated. 4.4.2 IMPACT OF AGENT-AWARE DRAFT-LENGTH CONTROL We measure the contribution of agent-aware draft-length control on SWE-bench Verified with Devstral  (Fig. 7)  . We use SAM-Decoding as the engine since its draft length is static cap, which lets the comparison reflect our control alone. Within AGSPEC-SAM, we compare our control against fixed caps, {8, 32}, and separately ablate the online scale. Figure 7: Draft-length control on SWE-bench Verified with Devstral. (a) Generation throughput (top) and AL (bottom) of fixed draft lengths (every agent capped at K, no online scale) and AGSPEC, normalized to = 8 within each group. (b) Mean draft tokens per drafting step by turn at batch size 1, split into accepted (solid) and rejected (hatched) tokens. (c) Fixed = 32 without and with the online scale enabled, at batch size 16: throughput (left) and case study of coder call per decoding step (right), with accepted tokens solid and rejected tokens lightly shaded. Fig. 7(a) shows that the benefit of long drafts disappears at large batch sizes. At batch size 1, = 32 is 14% faster than = 8, but at batch size 16 it is 30% slower, as rejected tokens consume compute shared by the whole batch. AGSPEC is the fastest at both batch sizes, 25% and 16% above = 8. = 32 attains higher AL than AGSPEC at batch size 1 (6.0 vs. 5.5) and slightly lower AL at batch size 16 (10.3 vs. 10.4), but remains slower at both batch sizes because of the drafts it rejects. Fig. 7(b) explains this at batch size 1. Rejected tokens add verification cost without producing output, so throughput depends on accepting many tokens while rejecting few. = 32 rejects 1126 tokens per step, whereas AGSPEC rejects at most 6, close to = 8, while still accepting 8389% as many tokens as = 32. AGSPEC lengthens its drafts only as reusable text accumulates, from about 10 tokens in early turns to 21 in the fifth, and thus achieves the highest throughput. Fig. 7(c) isolates the online scale at batch size 16. To measure its effect alone, we enable only the online scale on top of the fixed = 32 draft length of Fig. 7(a), without per-agent caps. The online scale alone raises throughput by 66%, as the share of rejected draft tokens falls from 78% to 50%. The example coder call shows how: without it, the drafter spends about 26 tokens per step over the first 160 steps but has fewer than 2 accepted; with it, the drafter shortens its drafts to about 4 tokens there and expands to the full draft length once the coder starts copying reusable text. It thus rejects 81.1% fewer tokens while taking only 11 more steps.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We proposed AGSPEC, retrieval-based SD framework for coding-agent pipelines. AGSPEC has two key designs: it makes the text an agent reuses available for retrieval in the form the agent emits, and it adapts the draft length to each agent using profiled accept lengths and verification feedback. Because AGSPEC is orthogonal to the retrieval engine, it can run on top of existing engines

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: without modification. Our evaluation shows that AGSPEC achieves the highest throughput in most evaluated settings on SWE-bench Verified and TeamBench, reaching 2.274.37 the throughput of autoregressive decoding at batch size 1, and remains effective without repository or explicit agent roles. These results show that retrieval-based SD for coding agents should follow the agent pipeline, as AGSPEC does: it indexes the text the session has produced, in the form agents emit it, and drafts as much as each agent can reuse.

sections.title: USE OF GENERATIVE AI TOOLS
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with translation, drafting and editing manuscript text, and providing feedback on figures and the presentation of our methods and experiments. Also, we exploited AI to get advice for the justification of our online adaptation mentioned at G.1. The authors reviewed AI-assisted suggestions and take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: AGSPEC verifies drafts with the target model, preserving its output distribution for each model call. Its decoding method therefore does not introduce new output-level behavior relative to ordinary target-model decoding. The additional concern is that the workspace and session corpus may contain sensitive prompts, repository content, or tool outputs. Deployments should restrict access to each sessions corpus, prevent its disclosure to other sessions, and discard it when the session ends.

sections.content: G.1 INTERPRETING THE SCALE UPDATE Fix an agent and drop the superscript (ai). We idealize the draft length as Di = αmi, ignoring rounding, clipping of α, the cap Kmax, and corpus continuations shorter than αmi. Let Ri be the number of tokens the target would accept from an unbounded draft, so that Ai = min(Ri, Di) and I[Ai < Di] = I[Ri < αmi] = I[Ui < α], Ui = Ri/mi. Objective. The loss is defined on the normalized length Ui because α scales the draft relative to the match length. Applying it to the raw length instead, ρτ (Ri αmi), yields the subgradient mi(τ I[Ri < αmi]), which weights each step by mi and targets an m-weighted quantile of ; Equation (3) does not apply this weighting. If the distribution of Ui were stationary, the expected update η (τ Pr[U < α]) Equilibrium. would vanish exactly when Pr[U < α] = τ , i.e., when drafts are fully accepted (Ai = Di) with probability 1 τ . In practice, η is fixed, sessions are finite, and the distribution of Ui shifts as Ss grows, so α does not converge; it fluctuates around and tracks this moving target. The ignored effects further perturb this balance. In particular, fully accepted draft truncated by Kmax reveals only Ri Kmax, not whether Ui α; counting it as full acceptance would bias α upward, which is why AGSPEC skips such updates. G.2 ADAPTIVE DRAFT LENGTH BEYOND RETRIEVAL Adaptive draft length has been studied mainly for model-based SD, where draft model or head generates each token and exposes signals about how likely that token is to be accepted. SpecDec++ trains an acceptance-prediction head and stops drafting once the predicted rejection probability exceeds threshold (Huang et al., 2025). DISCO feeds the draft models top-k probabilities and entropy to small classifier that decides whether to continue (Mamou et al., 2024), and AdaEDL and SVIP stop when the entropy of the draft distribution signals low acceptance probability (Agrawal et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). EAGLE-2 likewise expands its draft tree along the draft models most confident branches (Li et al., 2024). Retrieval-based SD has none of these signals. Its drafter copies continuation from corpus instead of sampling one, so there is no token distribution, entropy, or hidden state to read, and training head to predict acceptance would reintroduce the model that retrieval-based SD avoids. What retrieval drafter does have is the match itself, such as its length, occurrence count, and source corpus, and the outcome of verification. Existing retrieval methods either fix the draft length or scale it with the match length (2.2). SmartSpec uses verification outcomes, choosing the length that maximizes estimated goodput under the observed acceptance and system load (Liu et al., 2024), but it targets general request streams rather than agent pipelines, where acceptance differs systematically across agents. AGSPEC uses both available signals and adds the one that coding agents provide, the agent issuing each call: an offline cap per agent bounds the draft, and an online scale fitted to verification feedback sizes it from the match length. G.3 OVERHEAD OF AGSPEC Memory. The global corpus is loaded once per server and shared across sessions. Its resident host-memory footprint is 2.54.3 GB, with 915 load time  (Table 7)  ; it does not consume GPU memory or reduce the KV cache.
